```{r, include = FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
```

Thirty-nine of the forty-nine exported functions, exercised in the order of a real workflow,
on data simulated in the document itself. The help pages document the ten that the
tour leaves out. They are the inference helpers `se_function()` and `profile_theta()`,
`qc_phenotypes()`, `parentage_check()`, `h_inverse()`, `read_blupf90_snp()`,
`estimate_gamma()`, `half_t()`, `mcmc_diagnostics()` and the `_mt` twin of
`eval_internal()`. The test suite runs all of them. Each chunk runs at build time, so this
walkthrough cannot drift away from the code. The companion vignette ("from data to
breeding value") tells the story; this one is the tool bench.

## Step 0: simulate a population to work on

`simulate_breeding()` gene-drops haplotypes, so the genotypes it emits are consistent
with the pedigree it emits: one honest generator for every example.

```{r}
library(BreedingR)
s <- simulate_breeding(n_founders = 40, n_generations = 2,
                       offspring_per_generation = 80, h2 = 0.4,
                       n_markers = 200, seed = 7)
str(s, max.level = 1)
```

## Step 1: the pedigree toolbox

```{r}
p <- pedigree(s$pedigree)      # topological order + Meuwissen-Luo (1992) inbreeding
head(p, 3)
ai <- a_inverse(s$pedigree)    # Henderson's (1976) sparse A^-1, as triplets i/j/x/n
str(ai[c("i", "j", "x", "n")])
```

`a22_inverse()` takes 1-based positions in the topological order of `pedigree()`:

```{r}
gid <- s$genotypes$ids[141:200]
a22i <- a22_inverse(s$pedigree, geno = match(gid, p$id))
dim(a22i)
```

A pedigree whose third column holds the MATERNAL GRANDSIRE is declared, never guessed:
read as a dam, the grandsire would enter with weight 1/2 where the grandsire rules give
1/4 (Mrode and Pocrnic, 2023, secs. 3.6 and 3.7), and no check downstream could see it.
`sire_mgs()` declares it, the declaration travels to every fitter, and a third column
named `mgs` that was not declared is an error:

```{r}
bulls <- data.frame(id = c("s1", "s2", "s3", "s4"), sire = c("0", "0", "s1", "s3"),
                    mgs = c("0", "0", "s2", "s2"))
pedigree(sire_mgs(bulls))                  # s4: F = 1/16 through the grandsire s2
```

## Step 2: fit the base animal model, read everything out of it

```{r}
fit <- model(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree)
fit
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
round(h2(fit), 3)                           # simulated truth: 0.4
```

`h2()` takes the numerator by name and divides by the phenotypic variance of the trait:
the variances and covariances. In an animal model it is the `share` of `var(animal)` in
the printed table.

The fixed effects travel in the same solution vector, named `term=level`. The
parametrization is the implicit intercept with dropped columns at zero, so a table from
another convention (the book's, BLUPF90's) agrees only on CONTRASTS between levels:

```{r}
coef(fit, effects = "fixed")                # the same vector as fit$b
```

```{r}
e <- ebv(fit)                               # named vector, all pedigree animals
acc <- accuracy(fit, s$pedigree)            # with the (1+F) in the denominator
round(cor(e[names(s$tbv)], s$tbv), 2)       # against the simulator's own truth
summary(acc)
head(solutions(fit, s$pedigree), 3)         # id, ebv, se, acc, sorted by ebv
```

## Step 3: the formula markers, one by one

Repeated records ask for a permanent environment; `random()` is the iid effect for
litter or batch; a missing-value code leaves the likelihood via `missing_code=`:

```{r}
d3 <- s$data[rep(1:nrow(s$data), each = 2), ]
d3$y <- d3$y + rnorm(nrow(d3), 0, 0.5)
d3$y[1] <- -999
d3$lot <- sample(sprintf("lot%02d", 1:20), nrow(d3), TRUE)
f4 <- model(y ~ cg + random(lot) + animal(id) + pe(id), d3, s$pedigree,
            missing_code = -999)
round(f4$theta, 3)
```

A `random()` with fewer than five levels warns that its variance is barely determined;
three lots, or a litter numbered by parity, would.

The full maternal model of Mrode and Pocrnic (2023, Eqn 8.1): direct and maternal genetic share
ONE covariance matrix via `group=`, and there is ONE permanent environment, the dam's,
which carries her non-additive maternal genetics as well. `d5` has two records per
animal, so a second `pe()` on the animal itself is identifiable here too; on one record
per animal it would BE the residual. Two `pe()` in one model must be NAMED:

```{r}
d5 <- d3
d5$dam <- s$pedigree$dam[match(d5$id, s$pedigree$id)]
d5 <- d5[d5$dam != "0", ]
f5 <- model(y ~ cg + animal(id, group = "g") + maternal(dam, group = "g") +
              pe(id, nome = "pe_animal") + pe(dam, nome = "pe_dam"),
            d5, s$pedigree, missing_code = -999)
names(f5$theta)
```

The reaction norm is `rn()` over a basis you build with `legendre()`; `h2_curve()` and
`plot()` then read h2 along the gradient, and `h2()` refuses the fit, because here the
heritability is a function of the gradient and not one number. The `pe(id)` beside the
norm needs repeated records: with one record per animal it IS the residual, and the fit
says SINGULAR and names the two. So the example reuses the two records per animal of
`d3`, each at its own THI:

```{r}
d6 <- d3
d6$thi <- runif(nrow(d6), 55, 80)
d6 <- cbind(d6, legendre(d6$thi, order = 1, limits = c(55, 80)))
f6 <- model(y ~ cg + rn(id, base = c("phi0", "phi1")) + pe(id), d6, s$pedigree,
            missing_code = -999)
head(h2_curve(f6, limits = c(55, 80), points = 5))
plot(f6, limits = c(55, 80))
```

A sire model uses `sire()` when only males carry the genetic term. Unknown-parent
groups enter as metafounders (Legarra et al., 2015): a parent label with no line of its own,
declared with its gamma:

```{r}
ped8 <- s$pedigree
ped8$sire[ped8$sire == "0"] <- "L1"
ped8$dam[ped8$dam == "0"] <- "L2"
f8 <- model(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, ped8,
            metafounders = c("L1", "L2"), gamma = c(0.7, 0.7))
f8$converged
```

## Step 4: genomics, from files and QC to the single step

`read_plink()` reads the binary trio (or a .raw); here we write a tiny .bed by hand so
the example carries its own truth:

```{r}
pref <- file.path(tempdir(), "toy")
codes <- c(`2` = 0L, `1` = 2L, `0` = 3L)                 # 2 bits per genotype
pack <- function(g) { v <- codes[as.character(g)]
  sum(v * 4L^(seq_along(v) - 1L)) }
con <- file(paste0(pref, ".bed"), "wb")
writeBin(as.raw(c(0x6c, 0x1b, 0x01, pack(c(2, 1, 0, 2)), pack(c(0, 0, 1, 1)))), con)
close(con)
writeLines(sprintf("F%d I%d 0 0 0 -9", 1:4, 1:4), paste0(pref, ".fam"))
writeLines(sprintf("1 SNP%d 0 %d A B", 1:2, 1:2), paste0(pref, ".bim"))
read_plink(pref)$m
```

`qc_genotypes()` filters animals and markers by call rate, markers by MAF and
(optionally) HWE, and reports what each filter removed: silent filtering is how panels
lose the markers that mattered.

```{r}
q <- qc_genotypes(s$genotypes, min_call_rate = 0.9, min_maf = 0.05)
c(animals = length(q$ids), kept = ncol(q$m), by_call = q$n_call, by_maf = q$n_maf)
```

The APY core can be chosen by rule: `apy_core_select()` counts the eigenvalues of G that
explain 98% of its trace (Pocrnic et al., 2016) and draws that many animals at random
with a recorded seed, and `apy_core = "auto"` does the same inside a fit. On a genotyped
set this small the rule asks for nearly every animal, and the function warns when one
factorization with the core costs more than half of the exact one; `size =` overrides
the count and the table of counts is still reported:

```{r}
gen <- list(ids = gid, m = s$genotypes$m[141:200, ])
core <- apy_core_select(gen, size = 25)
core
```

The single step is an argument, not a function: `genotypes=` upgrades A to H. The
inverse of G* is exact by default, and `apy_core=` uses a global core:

```{r}
fss <- model(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree, genotypes = gen)
fap <- model(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree, genotypes = gen,
             apy_core = core)
round(c(apy = cor(ebv(fss, "animal"), ebv(fap, "animal"))), 3)
fss$dense_block                             # the k of the k^3 each factorization pays
```

Without `apy_core=` the dense block of the factor holds at least every genotyped animal,
and the fill of the pedigree can add to it.

The standalone inverse exposes the same approximation with its diagnostics (the
Mendelian/conditional residual of each animal), and `g_matrix()` builds the raw
VanRaden G of the book's examples (no blend, no A22 adjustment):

```{r}
ap <- apy_inverse(gen$m, core = 1:30)
G  <- g_matrix(gen)
c(min_apy_res = round(min(ap$mendeliano), 3), diag_G = round(mean(diag(G)), 3))
```

Marker effects come out of a single-step fit by backsolving, or directly by fitting the
markers as equations with `snp_blup()`, the path that never builds G (theta is GIVEN, the
routine-evaluation flow):

```{r}
a_hat <- snp_effects(fss, s$pedigree, gen)
fsnp <- snp_blup(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree, gen,
                 theta = unname(fss$theta))
round(cor(unclass(a_hat), fsnp$g[!is.na(fsnp$g)]), 3)
```

`pegs()` is the multi-environment route of Xavier and Habier (2022): no mixed model
equations, no relationship matrix, the effects of one marker for every environment solved
together by randomized Gauss-Seidel. It assumes the residuals of different environments are
independent, which holds when each animal is recorded in one place; for traits of the same
record, `model_mt()`. Here the herds of the simulated data stand in for environments.
It is ONE trait, so every true correlation is 1; with 60 animals split three ways the
estimates below are noise, which is what pseudo-expectation gives on data this small
(the method needs thousands of animals to pin `r_g` down):

```{r}
set.seed(1)
pg <- pegs(s$data[s$data$id %in% gid, ], "y", "id", gen, environment = "cg")
round(pg$Gcor, 2)
```

## Step 5: multi-trait

`cbind()` on the left, full R0, missingness handled record by record; `rg()` reads the
genetic correlation:

```{r}
dmt <- s$data
dmt$y2 <- 5 + 0.5 * s$tbv[dmt$id] + rnorm(nrow(dmt), 0, 0.8)
fmt <- model_mt(cbind(y, y2) ~ cg + animal(id), dmt, s$pedigree)
round(rg(fmt, "animal", "y", "y2"), 2)
head(ebv(fmt, "animal", trait = "y2"), 3)
```

## Step 6: the Bayesian half

`gibbs()` samples the SAME models; `ess()` and `geweke_z()` are the chain diagnostics
(also computed automatically on the result). With `theta_fixed=` it samples only the
locations, the mode whose posterior mean must be the BLUP. Left unset, the prior is the
hierarchical half-t of `half_t()` on a scalar term such as `animal(id)` here, `"flat"` on a
covariance group and on the residual, and the interweaving step of Yu and
Meng (2011) runs on every estimated term (`asis`); `prior =` puts one prior on every term
(`"jeffreys"`, `"flat"`, `"uniform_sd"`, `"half_t"` or a proper `c(df =, scale =)`) and
leaves that step off, and `family = "probit"` samples a binary trait on its liability, where
the default prior is `half_t(df = 4)` with a normal prior on the fixed effects and the
PX-DA move (`px`).
`summary()` gives the posterior quantiles and the heritability computed draw by draw.
`chains = 3` runs independent chains (their seeds come from `set.seed()`, and `cores =`
runs them at the same time with the same result), pools them, and adds `rhat()`, the
rank-normalized split R-hat of Vehtari et al. (2021):

```{r}
gb <- gibbs(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree,
            n_iter = 2000, burnin = 400, thin = 4, chains = 3)
summary(gb)
round(c(ess = ess(gb$chain_samples[[1]][, "var(animal)"]),
        geweke = geweke_z(gb$chain_samples[[1]][, "var(animal)"]),
        rhat = rhat(sapply(gb$chain_samples, function(m) m[, "var(animal)"]))), 3)
```

## Step 7: selection decisions

```{r}
idx <- selection_index(list(y = ebv(fit, "animal"),
                            y2 = ebv(fmt, "animal", trait = "y2")),
                       weights = c(y = 2, y2 = 1))
head(idx, 3)
drift <- rank_drift(ebv(fit, "animal"), ebv(fss, "animal"), top = 50)
c(spearman = round(drift$spearman, 3), retention = drift$retention)
```

## Step 8: the environmental axis

```{r}
round(thi(c(22, 30), c(60, 85)), 1)          # NRC 1971
heat_load(c(60, 70, 76), threshold = 68)     # zero in comfort, linear above
```

## Step 9: the exposed internals

The internals are exported for the gates, and they double as sparse tools: the same
triplet list `i/j/x/n` that `a_inverse()` returns feeds all three:

```{r}
ch <- sparse_chol(ai)                        # minimum degree (George & Liu 1989; dense
                                             # nodes set aside as in AMD) + symbolic + factor
x1 <- sparse_solve(ai, rep(1, ai$n))         # SOLVES A^-1 x = 1, so x = A %*% 1: the
                                             # row sums of A, without ever forming A
si <- selected_inverse(ai)                   # A at the factor's pattern (PEV reads this)
round(c(logdet = ch$logdet, x1_first = x1[1]), 3)
inv_pd(matrix(c(4, 1, 1, 3), 2))             # dense positive-definite inverse
br_version()
br_threads()                                 # OpenMP threads of the dense tail (default 1)
```

And `eval_internal()` (with its `_mt` twin) evaluates -2logL by the TWO
independent routes at any theta: the identity every gate in the package leans on.

```{r}
ev <- eval_internal(y ~ cg + animal(id), s$data, s$pedigree, theta = c(0.4, 0.6))
round(abs(ev$neg2logl - ev$neg2logl_V), 10)
```

## Step 10: the observed and the liability scale

`h2_observed()` and `h2_liability()` are the Dempster and Lerner conversion between the
0/1 observed scale and the liability scale: at incidence 0.234 half the heritability
is scale, not biology.

```{r}
round(c(observed = h2_observed(0.1781, 0.234),
        liability = h2_liability(0.0934, 0.234)), 4)
```

## The rule behind the tour

A new model is almost never a new function: it is a marker inside the formula of one
engine. A sibling fitter exists only when the mathematics changes: `model_mt()` (the
residual becomes R0), `gibbs()` (the algorithm samples instead of maximizing) and
`snp_blup()` (a fixed-components solver with markers as equations). Everything else
orbits the fit.
